subtopic: Reaching a fitness or sports goal
subtype: Approach: process goals when results stall [Revision]
passage: At the athletics club, Shreya checked the stopwatch again: 14.2 seconds for the hundred metres, the same as the last five weeks. She kicked the starting block and sat on the track. Coach Sarika ma'am crouched beside her. “What is the clock telling you?” “That I'm stuck.” “What can you control?” Shreya thought. “Coming to every session. Doing the start drill properly. Keeping my arms low.” Sarika ma'am handed her a card. “Track those, not the time. Tick each one.” For a month Shreya ticked boxes for attendance, the start drill and arm position, and stopped staring at the clock. In the fifth week she ran 14.0, and hardly noticed she'd stopped worrying.

qa.q: What did Shreya start tracking instead of her time?
qa.a: Attendance, the start drill and arm position.

qa.q: How did Shreya feel about her stalled sprint time?
qa.a: Stuck and frustrated: she kicked the starting block and sat down on the track.

qa.q: What else could Shreya do to check her technique, and why?
qa.a: Have a friend film her start each week, since seeing the drill helps her correct what the clock cannot show.

qa.q: How does the change look to Sarika ma'am?
qa.a: Sarika ma'am sees a runner fixed on the stopwatch and steers her toward things she can control, so she can stay motivated between improvements.

grounding: After a plateau in her sprint time, a student tracks attendance and technique drills, and progress returns.

passage:
Dear Payal Didi,
You asked me to write when something changed, so here it is.
For six weeks my 100 m time was stuck. Every Saturday I timed myself, and every Saturday it was the same, or worse. I started dreading practice. I even thought of quitting sprints.
Then I remembered what you said at the camp: “You can't control the stopwatch. You can control what you do.” So I stopped timing myself every week. Instead I made a chart with two questions: did I turn up, and did I do the start drills and arm drills properly? Every practice, two ticks or not.
For four weeks I just collected ticks. Nineteen practices out of twenty. Last Saturday Coach timed us for the district list, and I ran faster than I ever have.
I'm keeping the chart. Thank you for the advice.
Pema

qa.q: How many practices did Pema attend out of twenty?
How was Pema feeling during the six stuck weeks?
qa.a: Pema felt discouraged, dreading practice and even thinking of quitting sprints.

qa.q: What else could Pema add to the chart now that times are improving?
qa.a: A note on sleep and how rested each practice felt, to see what else helps, while still not timing every week.

qa.q: How might Payal Didi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Payal Didi would likely feel proud and touched that the advice from camp helped Pema through the plateau.

grounding: Shows a sprinter stuck on a plateau shifting from weekly timing to tracking attendance and technique drills, and seeing progress return within a month.

subtopic: Reaching a fitness or sports goal

passage:
Leela, you asked how I got faster this year. I'm Gopika, and here's the boring secret: I stopped looking at my time.
Last summer my 200 m was stuck for two months. Same time, every Saturday. I'd cry in the changing room, then train harder, then run the same time again. My coach finally took the stopwatch away from me. Not joking, she put it in her bag.
She said, “For four weeks you have two goals. Come to every session. And do the drills: starts, high knees, arm swing, all properly.” So I kept a small notebook: attendance, drills, a tick for each. It felt like nothing. Like homework, not racing.
At the end of the month she timed me. I'd dropped time for the first time since spring. And the month after that, again.
So now I only look at the stopwatch once a month. The rest of the time, I look at my ticks.

qa.q: Where did the coach put the stopwatch?
How did Gopika feel during the two stuck months?
qa.a: Gopika felt frustrated and upset, crying in the changing room and pushing harder without results.

qa.q: Why did the process goals work better than chasing times?
qa.a: They focused on what Gopika could control, turning up and doing the drills well, which built the skills that times depend on.

qa.q: How might the coach have felt taking the stopwatch away?
qa.a: The coach was probably worried about Gopika's distress and confident that shifting the focus to the process would help.

grounding: Shows a sprinter stuck on a plateau switching from chasing times to tracking attendance and technique drills, and seeing progress return the next month.
